facts.text: **The main finding** is that only one source spells out the "8-paragraph skeleton": a commercial PR blog (Instant Press, 2026-05-02). Every other source describes op-ed structures with about 7 parts, about 5, or 12–16 paragraphs. None of them uses the number eight.

- **Does the paragraph count matter?** The skeleton fixes eight paragraphs (https://www.instantpress.co/blog/how-to-write-an-op-ed-for-media). A University of Minnesota template based on Harvard Kennedy School prescribes roughly 12–16 paragraphs: 2–3 opening, 4–5 context, 4–5 solutions, 1–2 counterargument, and 1 conclusion (https://umarcomm.umn.edu/blog/2025/06/02/how-structure-your-op-ed). Pinkston calls for 3–6 short body paragraphs (https://pinkston.co/how-to-write-an-op-ed/). In scope: where the op-ed paragraph skeleton comes from, its dated appearances, its official wording, and the variants that disagree with it. The skeleton is lede, thesis, three argument points, a "to be sure" paragraph, and a conclusion.

- **Primary sources:** two peer-reviewed meta-analyses (O'Keefe 1999; O'Keefe & Hoeken 2021) and the dated HKS primary handout (Seglin, 2017). - **Disconfirming sources sought and found:** O'Keefe & Hoeken 2021, the paragraph-length arithmetic, the HKS/Harris placement variants, and the CMA no-counterargument template. - **Weakest link:** the only source that literally specifies "8 paragraphs" is a single commercial blog (Instant Press, 2026).
